source.title: Can Dialects Be Steered Like Languages? Sparse Neurons and Distributed Directions in Arabic LLMs
source.authors: K. Elozeiri; Mervat T. Abassy; Omar Kallas; Fahim Dalvi; Preslav Nakov; Kentaro Inui; Nadir Durrani

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether dialect representations in Arabic LLMs are localized in selected neurons or distributed in residual space, and reports that selected neurons cover only part of the dialect direction. This refines the representation claim in a new setting, rather than reproducing the original toy-model method.
record.gate_note: The residual-subspace coverage analysis directly measures overlap between selected neuron subspaces and dialect directions. Steering-performance results are not included as rows because they measure output quality and dialect control, not the spatial distribution of represented features. Results attributed to cited prior work and values used only to choose steering settings are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study never addresses superposition. It motivates vector steering by assuming dialect features 'may be distributed across many neurons' and then measures something else. Its central measure asks how much of a contrastive dialect-minus-MSA mean-difference vector lies in the span of the down-projection columns of LAPE-selected MLP neurons. That vector is a related but different construct. It is not a recovered sparse feature, and the measure does not show whether individual features are spread across many neurons. Low coverage mostly reflects dimensional share: the selected neurons are under 1% of MLP dimensions, and matched random subsets reach similar coverage (e.g., ALLaM RAB 19.34% vs 18.90%). No SAE is used and no toy model is trained. The finding is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that dialect information is both sparse and distributed: LAPE neurons (under 1% of MLP dimensions, concentrated in late layers) capture only a partial projection of the residual dialect direction. Vector steering controls dialect more reliably, and neuron steering cannot induce dialect from MSA prompts. They also note that the selected neurons beat random subsets in coverage reliably for Fanar but only for some ALLaM dialects.
record.recipe_differences: Measures residual-subspace coverage of LAPE-selected neuron output directions against contrastive dialect–MSA residual directions in Arabic LLMs; it does not use the original toy-network setup or its feature-sparsity sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Coverage varies by model and dialect; the authors report ALLaM's average coverage as 14.99% and Fanar's as 7.51%, with dialect-level variation in enrichment over matched random subsets.

fits_no_version.finding: LAPE-selected neurons cover 4.67%–20.55% of contrastive dialect steering directions. Coverage is enriched over matched random neuron subsets for all six Fanar dialects but only for some ALLaM dialects (CAI, BEI clearly; RAB about the same as random). Vector steering outperforms neuron steering, and neuron steering fails to induce dialect from MSA prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contrastive concept/steering directions in LLM residual streams are only partially spanned by the output weights of selectively-active neurons, and the share captured exceeds random neuron sets only in some settings.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to two Arabic-centric instruction-tuned models and a selected set of dialects. The authors state that the relationship between localized neuron representations and distributed residual-space features remains partially understood. Some ALLaM dialect coverage results are not reliably above matched random-subset baselines.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the row limit.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, or feature geometry.
No capacity or feature-importance analysis; polysemanticity is not measured.
No analysis of the causes of polysemantic neurons.
No SAE or dictionary learning. No measure of whether individual features are distributed across many neurons; only steering-vector coverage by a selected neuron span.
Feature dimensionality is not studied; dialect is treated as a single mean-difference direction by construction.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 linkage overreads the study. The paper makes no reference to superposition, and its coverage metric is largely determined by subspace dimension, as the random-exclusion baselines show. The record also labeled every row 'observed', even where coverage is not above random (r4–r6).

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, more sparse features than dimensions, superposition geometry, and sparsity-dependent transitions.
Capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, and polysemantic neurons.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity and whether polysemantic neurons are evidence of superposition.
The study examines Arabic dialect directions in two Arabic-centric LLMs; it does not test SAE-recovered features, other feature types, or broader model populations.
SAE feature completeness, stability, and canonical status.
Whether superposed features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Both tested Arabic-centric models across the six evaluated dialects
reader_labels.reason: Selected-neuron subspaces cover only 4.67%–20.55% of the measured residual dialect directions, consistent with a substantial distributed component (r1–r14).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Dialect-specific neuron alignment, especially ALLaM DOH, RAB, and RIY
reader_labels.reason: Coverage and enrichment over matched random subsets vary by dialect and model; ALLaM's RAB coverage is near its random baseline, and several ALLaM dialect comparisons are not reliably enriched (r4–r6).
